title: Bloor v. Falstaff Brewing Corp.
summary: Falstaff’s best-efforts promise required attention to Ballantine’s sales volume; concentrating on Falstaff’s overall profits while allowing that volume to collapse did not satisfy the agreement.
notes:
The opinion connects the royalty arrangement to Wood v. Lucy: even without the express best-efforts language, a good-faith effort to generate royalty-producing sales would matter. The separate assigned Bloor agreement is not reproduced here in full; the casebook quotes the operative provisions. The notes offer several competing accounts of what “best” efforts require.

601 F.2d 609 (2d Cir. 1979), affirming 454 F. Supp. 258 (S.D.N.Y. 1978). The royalty ran from April 1972 to March 1978, and the two clauses at issue were the promise to use best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales and the liquidated payment triggered if Falstaff substantially discontinued distribution under the Ballantine name.

sections.Parties: Bloor, trustee for the former Ballantine business, sued Falstaff, which had purchased Ballantine’s brands and associated assets. The dispute concerned royalties, the express best-efforts covenant, and a separate stipulated-payment provision.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1972, Falstaff purchased Ballantine’s labels, trademarks, distribution system, and other assets, but not its brewery. The price was $4 million plus fifty cents per barrel sold during a six-year royalty period. Paragraph 8(a) required best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales. Another provision required specified payments if Falstaff substantially discontinued distribution of Ballantine beer.

Ballantine had a history of losses. Falstaff also experienced severe financial difficulty before new management and financing arrived in 1975. Its new controller emphasized cost cutting and profit. Ballantine advertising fell from roughly $1 million to $115,000 annually. Falstaff closed distribution depots, served fewer small accounts, chose a distributor with a competing brand, did not pursue a possible alternative distribution arrangement, and stopped setting sales goals. Its own brands did not carry the fifty-cent royalty. Ballantine’s sales declined much more sharply than useful regional comparisons, while Falstaff’s overall finances recovered. Ending illegal promotional practices was proper and was not an obligation to continue them.
sections.Procedural History: The district court found a breach of best efforts and awarded lost-royalty damages, but rejected the claim that the separate substantial-discontinuation provision had been triggered. Both parties appealed. The Second Circuit affirmed the judgment and the use of comparable regional brands to estimate damages.
sections.Issue: How far did the express best-efforts obligation constrain Falstaff’s business decisions, and did the record support liability and a reasonable estimate of lost royalties?
sections.Holding: The best-efforts covenant was breached. Falstaff did not have to bankrupt itself or incur substantial losses, but had to explore reasonable measures to maintain volume and give fair consideration to the royalty-producing business.
sections.Reasoning:
The royalty was part of the purchase price, so Falstaff’s decisions about promotion directly affected what the seller received. The express best-efforts covenant imposed a volume-oriented obligation beyond a freedom to maximize profit for Falstaff as a whole. Treating Ballantine no worse than Falstaff’s own brands was not necessarily sufficient: management could reduce volume on its own brands for profit reasons, but had separately promised efforts to preserve Ballantine volume.

After the immediate insolvency danger passed, Falstaff had to investigate measures that could slow the decline without financially disastrous costs. Evidence that it simply did not care about that volume supported breach and shifted the burden to show that no significant feasible measures were available. The appellate court rejected an inference from certain Texas and Missouri comparisons but found the remaining evidence sufficient.

Lost royalties could not be calculated with certainty. The court accepted a stable basis for estimation using the performance of Rheingold and Schaefer, comparable regional low-priced beers. It preserved the distinction between compensation for failing to use best efforts and the stipulated payment triggered by substantial discontinuation; proof of the former did not automatically prove the latter.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Bloor explains how a flexible business obligation can still be enforceable. It identifies the promised objective, considers the promisor’s financial capacity, examines concrete decisions, and gives a workable damages method.

topics.discretion: Promotional and distribution choices remained with Falstaff but were constrained by its promised sales-volume objective.
topics.good-faith: Self-interest could not erase the seller’s royalty interest in the purchased business.
topics.best-efforts: The court evaluates feasible promotional measures rather than demanding unlimited spending.
topics.damages-certainty: Comparable regional brands supplied a reasonable foundation for estimating lost royalties.
topics.stipulated-remedies: A breach of best efforts did not by itself trigger the separate substantial-discontinuation payment.
topics.implied-efforts: Bloor gives content to a best-efforts obligation in an exclusive arrangement, extending the Wood v. Lucy line.
topics.ucc306: UCC 2-306(2)'s best-efforts duty in exclusive dealings is the statutory analogue of the express clause construed here.
topics.certainty-damages: The court approved estimating lost royalties from the sales of comparable regional brands despite uncertainty.
